prompt.context: Our client is an office furniture manufacturer. They are concerned that their stock price is not growing as fast as their competitors'. Furthermore, the client's annual growth is 1% per year, while that of main competitors' is 10% per year. Also, our client's EBIT margin is 10% while competitors' EBIT is 20%.
prompt.question: What would be your recommendations for our client?

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: Market grows 1% per year. No overall market size information is available.

clarifying_info.q: What is our client's market share and who are the competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client is the market leader with 20% market share. The other three main competitors each have 10% market share. The rest is fragmented.

clarifying_info.q: How do our prices compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The 3 main competitors have prices that are 10% lower than ours.
The market is composed of two segments: Segment 1 - Fortune 500 companies (80% of our sales); Segment 2 - channel sales to small companies (20% of our sales). We do not own these channels.
Customers are looking for furniture that is hassle-free (i.e., universal, will fit in all offices, goes with each other, etc.).
Our product is viewed as being superior and we have a strong brand.

clarifying_info.q: What does our cost structure look like?
clarifying_info.a: Ignore fixed costs. Our COGS breaks down into materials (40%), direct labor (40%), overhead (20%). Assume competitors have the same material cost, overhead, and SG&A per product in dollars (not as a percentage of price). Nothing is known about competitor labor cost.

exhibits.title: Cost and Margin Table
exhibits.shows: A table comparing our client and competitor on price, COGS components (materials, labor, overhead), and EBIT margin
exhibits.data: Client price $100, EBIT margin 10% ($10); COGS materials 40% ($36 for both), overhead 20% ($18 for both); competitor price $90, EBIT margin 20% ($18); competitor labor cost unknown

framework: Market analysis: size, growth rate, trends, segments
Customer analysis: needs, segments (Fortune 500 vs. channel/small companies), buying criteria
Company analysis: product quality, brand, pricing, cost structure, market share
Competitor analysis: pricing, growth, cost structure differences
Competitive advantage: identify sources of cost disadvantage and growth gap, develop recommendations

questions.prompt: Calculate the competitor's labor cost per typical product. Assume our product sells for $100, competitors' price is 10% lower. Our COGS: materials 40%, labor 40%, overhead 20% of our price (i.e., $90 COGS on a $100 product). Competitor has same material, overhead, and SG&A in dollar terms. Competitor EBIT margin is 20%.
questions.guidance: A strong answer builds the comparison table from scratch without being given it. Candidate should recognize that both players have the same dollar-value material and overhead per unit, then solve for competitor labor as the residual. Key insight: competitor charges less but earns more — their labor cost must be substantially lower.

math.setup: Our price = $100, EBIT = 10% = $10, so total COGS+SGA = $90. Materials = 40% of $90 = $36; Labor = 40% of $90 = $36; Overhead = 20% of $90 = $18. Competitor price = $90, EBIT = 20% = $18, so total COGS+SGA = $72. Competitor materials = $36 (same); competitor overhead = $18 (same); solve for competitor labor.
steps: Labor cost advantage for competitor = $36 - $18 = $18 per unit
math.answer: Competitor labor cost = $18 per unit; they have an $18 labor cost advantage over our client.

questions.prompt: Why might competitors have lower labor costs, and what can be done about it operationally?
questions.guidance: Candidate should diagnose the root cause of the labor cost gap. Strong answers explore productivity differences (throughput rates vary across workers), process inefficiencies, and incentive structures. Candidate should generate several operational levers.

brainstorming.prompt: How can the client realize savings from the labor cost reduction and grow revenue given they do not want to lay off workers?

categories.name: Operations / Productivity improvements
ideas: Train less efficient workers to raise throughput
Resource pulling: pull workers from bottleneck steps to balance production line
Resource reallocation: match workers to tasks where they are most productive
Build separate production lines by worker efficiency tier
Provide less efficient workers with better tools or equipment

categories.name: Revenue growth to utilize freed capacity
ideas: Go into service business providing integrated solutions to Fortune 500 customers
Acquire one or two competitors to benefit from their higher growth rate and to utilize increased capacity
Increase sales efforts in existing segments
Explore channel partnerships to expand reach in the small-company segment

categories.name: Pricing / Positioning
ideas: Leverage superior brand and product quality to justify premium pricing
Evaluate whether a modest price reduction could capture share without destroying margin

categories.name: Incentive system
ideas: If capacity cannot be sold, redesign incentives so more efficient workers match output to demand rather than producing excess

recommendation: Address the $18/unit labor cost disadvantage by implementing operational improvements: train lower-productivity workers, reallocate resources, and where possible group workers by efficiency to balance production lines
Grow revenue to absorb the freed capacity — prioritize entering the integrated-solutions service business for Fortune 500 clients and evaluate selective acquisitions of higher-growth competitors
Maintain premium pricing and brand positioning; do not cut prices to match competitors unless revenue growth initiatives stall
risks: Labor productivity initiatives may face workforce resistance given the company's policy of paying above-market wages
Acquisitions carry integration risk and may not transfer the competitors' growth rates
Service business expansion requires new capabilities and may dilute manufacturing focus
next_steps: Conduct time-and-motion studies to quantify productivity variance across the workforce
Model the revenue uplift needed to fully utilize capacity freed by productivity gains
Assess acquisition targets among the three main competitors for strategic and cultural fit
Develop a roadmap for integrated-solutions offerings to Fortune 500 segment
